entries.38b8eec902220bb7e40c486110ddca1882cae804: <div sID="gen9013" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="4" osisID="Esth.4" sID="Esth.4"/> <div eID="gen9013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9014" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen9015" type="x-p"/> We left God's Isaac bound upon the altar and ready to be sacrificed, and the enemies triumphing in the prospect of it; but things here begin to work towards a deliverance, and they begin at the right end. I. The Jews' friends lay to heart the danger and lament it, <reference osisRef="Esth.4.1-Esth.4.4">ver. 1-4</reference>. II. Matters are concerted between Mordecai and Esther for the preventing of it. 1. Esther enquires into this case, and receives a particular account of it, <reference osisRef="Esth.4.5-Esth.4.7">ver. 5-7</reference>. 2. Mordecai urges her to intercede with the king for a revocation of the edict, <reference osisRef="Esth.4.8-Esth.4.9">ver. 8, 9</reference>. III. Esther objects the danger of addressing the king uncalled, <reference osisRef="Esth.4.10-Esth.4.12">ver. 10-12</reference>. IV. Mordecai presses her to venture, <reference osisRef="Esth.4.13-Esth.4.14">ver. 13, 14</reference>. V. Esther, after a religious fast of three days, promises to do so (<reference osisRef="Esth.4.15-Esth.4.17">ver. 15-17</reference>), and we shall find that she sped well.
entries.b93cec54a02e281d33071ae073f45bcea680b157: <div eID="gen9015" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen9014" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Great Mourning among the Jews. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 510.)</title> <div sID="gen9016" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> When Mordecai perceived all that was done, Mordecai rent his clothes, and put on sackcloth with ashes, and went out into the midst of the city, and cried with a loud and a bitter cry; <hi type="super">2</hi> And came even before the king's gate: for none <hi type="italic">might</hi> enter into the king's gate clothed with sackcloth. <hi type="super">3</hi> And in every province, whithersoever the king's commandment and his decree came, <hi type="italic">there was</hi> great mourning among the Jews, and fasting, and weeping, and wailing; and many lay in sackcloth and ashes. <hi type="super">4</hi> So Esther's maids and her chamberlains came and told <hi type="italic">it</hi> her. Then was the queen exceedingly grieved; and she sent raiment to clothe Mordecai, and to take away his sackcloth from him: but he received <hi type="italic">it</hi> not. <div eID="gen9016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9017" type="x-p"/> Here we have an account of the general sorrow that there was among the Jews upon the publishing of Haman's bloody edict against them. It was a sad time with the church. 1. Mordecai cried bitterly, <hi type="italic">rent his clothes, and put on sackcloth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Esth.4.1-Esth.4.2">v. 1, 2</reference>. He not only thus vented his grief, but proclaimed it, that all might take notice of it that he was not ashamed to own himself a friend to the Jews, and a fellow-sufferer with them, their brother and companion in tribulation, how despicable and how odious soever they were now represented by Haman's faction. It was nobly done thus publicly to espouse what he knew to be a righteous cause, and the cause of God, even when it seemed a desperate and a sinking cause. Mordecai laid the danger to heart more than any because he knew that Haman's spite was against him primarily, and that it was for his sake that the rest of the Jews were struck at; and therefore, though he did not repent of what some would call his obstinacy, for he persisted in it (<reference osisRef="Esth.5.9">ch. v. 9</reference>), yet it troubled him greatly that his people should suffer for his scruples, which perhaps occasioned some of them to reflect upon him as too precise. But, being able to appeal to God that what he did he did from a principle of conscience, he could with comfort commit his own cause and that of his people to him that judgeth righteously. God will keep those that are exposed by the tenderness of their consciences. Notice is here taken of a law that <hi type="italic">none might enter into the king's gate clothed with sackcloth;</hi> though the arbitrary power of their kings often, as now, set many a mourning, yet none must come near the king in a mourning dress, because he was not willing to hear the complaints of such. Nothing but what was gay and pleasant must appear at court, and every thing that was melancholy must be banished thence; all in king's palaces <hi type="italic">wear soft clothing</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.11.8">Matt. xi. 8</reference>), not sackcloth. But thus to keep out the badges of sorrow, unless they could withal have kept out the causes of sorrow—to forbid sackcloth to enter, unless they could have forbidden sickness, and trouble, and death to enter—was jest. However this obliged Mordecai to keep his distance, and only to come before the gate, not to take his place in the gate. 2. All the Jews in every province laid it much to heart, <reference osisRef="Esth.4.3">v. 3</reference>. They denied themselves the comfort of their tables (for they fasted and mingled tears with their meat and drink), and the comfort of their beds at night, for <hi type="italic">they lay in sackcloth and ashes.</hi> Those who for want of confidence in God, and affection to their own land, has staid in the land of their captivity, when Cyrus gave them liberty to be gone, now perhaps repented of their folly, and wished, when it was too late, that they had complied with the call of God. 3. Esther the queen, upon a general intimation of the trouble Mordecai was in, <hi type="italic">was exceedingly grieved,</hi> <reference osisRef="Esth.4.4">v. 4</reference>. Mordecai's grief was hers, such a respect did she still retain for him; and the Jews' danger was her distress; for, though a queen, she forgot not her relation to them. Let not the greatest think it below them to <hi type="italic">grieve for the affliction of Joseph,</hi> though they themselves be <hi type="italic">anointed with the chief ointments,</hi> <reference osisRef="Amos.6.6">Amos vi. 6</reference>. Esther sent change of raiment to Mordecai, the <hi type="italic">oil of joy for mourning and the garments of praise for the spirit of heaviness;</hi> but because he would make her sensible of the greatness of his grief, and consequently of the cause of it, <hi type="italic">he received it not,</hi> but was as one that refused to be comforted.
entries.ce3c917be911e311715b9b2d720c0a18e0b0f405: <div eID="gen9017" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Mordecai's Application to Esther; Esther Urged to Petition the King; Esther Resolves to Petition the King. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi>  510.)</title> <div sID="gen9018" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> Then called Esther for Hatach, <hi type="italic">one</hi> of the king's chamberlains, whom he had appointed to attend upon her, and gave him a commandment to Mordecai, to know what it <hi type="italic">was,</hi> and why it <hi type="italic">was.</hi> <hi type="super">6</hi> So Hatach went forth to Mordecai unto the street of the city, which <hi type="italic">was</hi> before the king's gate. <hi type="super">7</hi> And Mordecai told him of all that had happened unto him, and of the sum of the money that Haman had promised to pay to the king's treasuries for the Jews, to destroy them. <hi type="super">8</hi> Also he gave him the copy of the writing of the decree that was given at Shushan to destroy them, to show <hi type="italic">it</hi> unto Esther, and to declare <hi type="italic">it</hi> unto her, and to charge her that she should go in unto the king, to make supplication unto him, and to make request before him for her people. <hi type="super">9</hi> And Hatach came and told Esther the words of Mordecai. <hi type="super">10</hi> Again Esther spake unto Hatach, and gave him commandment unto Mordecai; <hi type="super">11</hi> All the king's servants, and the people of the king's provinces, do know, that whosoever, whether man or woman, shall come unto the king into the inner court, who is not called, <hi type="italic">there is</hi> one law of his to put <hi type="italic">him</hi> to death, except such to whom the king shall hold out the golden sceptre, that he may live: but I have not been called to come in unto the king these thirty days. <hi type="super">12</hi> And they told to Mordecai Esther's words. <hi type="super">13</hi> Then Mordecai commanded to answer Esther, Think not with thyself that thou shalt escape in the king's house, more than all the Jews. <hi type="super">14</hi> For if thou altogether holdest thy peace at this time, <hi type="italic">then</hi> shall there enlargement and deliverance arise to the Jews from another place; but thou and thy father's house shall be destroyed: and who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for <hi type="italic">such</hi> a time as this? <hi type="super">15</hi> Then Esther bade <hi type="italic">them</hi> return Mordecai <hi type="italic">this answer,</hi> <hi type="super">16</hi> Go, gather together all the Jews that are present in Shushan, and fast ye for me, and neither eat nor drink three days, night or day: I also and my maidens will fast likewise; and so will I go in unto the king, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> not according to the law: and if I perish, I perish. <hi type="super">17</hi> So Mordecai went his way, and did according to all that Esther had commanded him. <div eID="gen9018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9019" type="x-p"/> So strictly did the laws of Persia confine the wives, especially the king's wives, that it was not possible for Mordecai to have a conference with Esther about this important affair, but divers messages are here carried between them by Hatach, whom the king had appointed to attend her, and it seems he was one she could confide in. <div eID="gen9019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9020" type="x-p"/> I. She sent to Mordecai to know more particularly and fully what the trouble was which he was now lamenting (<reference osisRef="Esth.4.5">v. 5</reference>) and why it was that he would not put off his sackcloth. To enquire thus after news, that we may know the better how to direct our griefs and joys, our prayers and praises, well becomes all that love Sion. If we must weep with those that weep, we must know why they weep. <div eID="gen9020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9021" type="x-p"/> II. Mordecai sent her an authentic account of the whole matter, with a charge to her to intercede with the king in this matter: <hi type="italic">Mordecai told him all that had happened unto him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Esth.4.7">v. 7</reference>), what a pique Haman had against him for now bowing to him, and by what arts he had procured this edict; he sent her also a true copy of the edict, that she might see what imminent danger she and her people were in, and charged her, if she had any respect for him or any kindness for the Jewish nation, that she should appear now on their behalf, rectify the misinformations with which the king was imposed upon, and set the matter in a true light, not doubting but that then he would vacate the decree. <div eID="gen9021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9022" type="x-p"/> III. She sent her case to Mordecai, that she could not, without peril of her life, address the king, and that therefore he put a great hardship upon her in urging her to it. Gladly would she wait, gladly would she stoop, to do the Jews a kindness; but, if she must run the hazard of being put to death as a malefactor, she might well say, <hi type="italic">I pray thee have me excused,</hi> and find out some other intercessor. <div eID="gen9022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9023" type="x-p"/> 1. The law was express, and all knew it, that whosoever came to the king uncalled should be put to death, unless he was pleased to <hi type="italic">hold out the golden sceptre to them,</hi> and it was extremely doubtful whether she should find him in so good a humour, <reference osisRef="Esth.4.11">v. 11</reference>. This law was made, not so much in prudence, for the greater safety of the king's person, as in pride, that being seldom seen, and not without great difficulty, he might be adored as a little god. A foolish law it was; for, (1.) It made the kings themselves unhappy, confining them to their retirements for fear they should be seen. This made the royal palace little better than a royal prison, and the kings themselves could not but become morose, and perhaps melancholy, and so a terror to others and a burden to themselves. Many have their lives made miserable by their own haughtiness and ill nature. (2.) It was bad for the subjects; for what good had they of a king that they might never have liberty to apply to for the redress of grievances and appeal to from the inferior judges? It is not thus in the court of the King of kings; to the footstool of his throne of grace we may at any time <hi type="italic">come boldly,</hi> and may be sure of an answer of peace to the prayer of faith. We are welcome, not only into the inner court, but even into the holiest, through the blood of Jesus. (3.) It was particularly very uncomfortable for their wives (for there was not a proviso in the law to except them), who were <hi type="italic">bone of their bone</hi> and <hi type="italic">flesh of their flesh.</hi> But perhaps it was wickedly intended as much against them as any other, that the kings might the more freely enjoy their concubines, and Esther knew it. Miserable was the kingdom when the princes framed their laws to serve their lusts. <div eID="gen9023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9024" type="x-p"/> 2. Her case was at present very discouraging. Providence so ordered it that, just at this juncture, she was under a cloud, and the king's affections cooled towards her, for she had been <hi type="italic">kept from his presence thirty days,</hi> that her faith and courage might be the more tried, and that God's goodness in the favour she now found with the king notwithstanding might shine the brighter. It is probable that Haman endeavoured by women, as well as wine, to divert the king from thinking of what he had done, and then Esther was neglected, from whom no doubt he did what he could to alienate the king, knowing her to be averse to him. <div eID="gen9024" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9025" type="x-p"/> IV. Mordecai still insisted upon it that, whatever hazard she might run, she must apply to the king in this great affair, <reference osisRef="Esth.4.13-Esth.4.14">v. 13, 14</reference>. No excuse will serve, but she must appear an advocate in this cause; he suggested to her, 1. That it was her own cause, for that the decree to <hi type="italic">destroy all the Jews</hi> did not except her: "<hi type="italic">Think not</hi> therefore that <hi type="italic">thou shalt escape in the king's house,</hi> that the palace will be thy protection, and the crown save thy head: no, thou art a Jewess, and, if the rest be cut off, thou wilt be cut off too." It was certainly her wisdom rather to expose herself to a conditional death from her husband than to a certain death from her enemy. 2. That it was a cause which, one way or other, would certainly be carried, and which therefore she might safely venture in. "If thou shouldst decline the service, <hi type="italic">enlargement and deliverance will arise to the Jews from another place.</hi>" This was the language of a strong faith, which <hi type="italic">staggered not at the promise</hi> when the danger was most threatening, but <hi type="italic">against hope believed in hope.</hi> Instruments may fail, but God's covenant will not. 3. That if she deserted her friends now, through cowardice and unbelief, she would have reason to fear that some judgment from heaven would be the ruin of her and her family: "<hi type="italic">Thou and thy father's house shall be destroyed,</hi> when the rest of the families of the Jews shall be preserved." He that by sinful shifts will save his life, and cannot find in his heart to trust God with it in the way of duty, shall lose it in the way of sin. 4. That divine Providence had an eye to this in bringing her to be queen: "<hi type="italic">Who knows whether thou hast come to the kingdom for such a time as this?</hi>" and therefore, (1.) "Thou art bound in gratitude to do this service for God and his church, else thou dost not answer the end of thy elevation." (2.) "Thou needest not fear miscarrying in the enterprise; if God designed thee for it, he will bear thee out and give thee success." Now, [1.] It appeared, by the event, that she did come to the kingdom that she might be an instrument of the Jews' deliverance, so that Mordecai was right in the conjecture. <hi type="italic">Because the Lord loved his people,</hi> therefore he made Esther queen. There is a wise counsel and design in all the providences of God, which is unknown to us till it is accomplished, but it will prove, in the issue, that they are all intended for, and centre in, the good of the church. [2.] The probability of this was a good reason why she should now bestir herself, and do her utmost for her people. We should every one of us consider for what end God has put us in the place where we are, and study to answer that end; and, when any particular opportunity of serving God and our generation offers itself, we must take care that we do not let it slip; for we were entrusted with it that we might improve it. These things Mordecai urges to Esther; and some of the Jewish writers, who are fruitful in invention, add another thing which had <hi type="italic">happened to him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Esth.4.7">v. 7</reference>) which he desired she might be told, "that going home, the night before, in great heaviness, upon the notice of Haman's plot, he met three Jewish children coming from school, of whom he enquired what they had learned that day; one of them told him his lesson was, <reference osisRef="Prov.3.25-Prov.3.26">Prov. iii. 25, 26</reference>, <hi type="italic">Be not afraid of sudden fear;</hi> the second told him his was, <reference osisRef="Isa.8.10">Isa. viii. 10</reference>, <hi type="italic">Take counsel together, and it shall come to nought;</hi> the third told him his was <reference osisRef="Isa.46.4">Isa. xlvi. 4</reference>, <hi type="italic">I have made, and I will bear, even I will carry and will deliver you.</hi> 'O the goodness of God,' says Mordecai, 'who out of the mouth of babes and sucklings ordains strength!'" <div eID="gen9025" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9026" type="x-p"/> V. Esther hereupon resolved, whatever it might cost her, to apply to the king, but not till she and her friends had first applied to God. Let them first by fasting and prayer obtain God's favour, and then she should hope to find favour with the king, <reference osisRef="Esth.4.15-Esth.4.16">v. 15, 16</reference>. She speaks here, <div eID="gen9026" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9027" type="x-p"/> 1. With the piety and devotion that became an Israelite. She had here eye up unto God, in whose hands the hearts of kings are, and on whom she depended to incline this king's heart towards her. She went in peril of her life, but would think herself safe, and would be easy, when she had committed the keeping of her soul to God and had put herself under his protection. She believed that God's favour was to be obtained by prayer, that his people are a praying people, and he a prayer-hearing God. She knew it was the practice of good people, in extraordinary cases, to join fasting with prayer, and many of them to join together in both. She therefore, (1.) Desired that Mordecai would direct the Jews that were in Shushan to <hi type="italic">sanctify a fast</hi> and <hi type="italic">call a solemn assembly,</hi> to meet in the respective synagogues to which they belonged, and to pray for her, and to keep a solemn fast, abstaining from all set meals and all pleasant food for three days, and as much as possible from all food, in token of their humiliation for sin and in a sense of their unworthiness of God's mercy. Those know not how to value the divine favours who grudge thus much labour and self-denial in the pursuit of it. (2.) She promised that she and her family would sanctify this fast in her apartment of the palace, for she might not come to their assemblies; her maids were either Jewesses or so far proselytes that they joined with her in her fasting and praying. Here is a good example of a mistress praying with her maids, and it is worthy to be imitated. Observe also, Those who are confined to privacy may join their prayers with those of the solemn assemblies of God's people; those that are absent in body may be present in spirit. Those who desire, and have, the prayers of others for them, must not think that this will excuse them from praying for themselves. <div eID="gen9027" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9028" type="x-p"/> 2. With the courage and resolution that became a queen. "When we have sought God in this matter, <hi type="italic">I will go unto the king</hi> to intercede for my people. <hi type="italic">I know it is not according to the king's law,</hi> but it is according to God's law; and therefore, whatever comes of it, I will venture, and not count my life dear to me, so that I may serve God and his church, and, <hi type="italic">if I perish, I perish.</hi> I cannot lose my life in a better cause. Better do my duty and die for my people than shrink from my duty and die with them." She reasons as the lepers (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.7.4">2 Kings vii. 4</reference>): "<hi type="italic">If I sit still, I die;</hi> if I venture, I may live, and be the life of my people: if the worst come to the worst," as we say, "<hi type="italic">I shall but die.</hi>" Nothing venture, nothing win. She said not this in despair or passion, but in a holy resolution to do her duty and trust God with the issue; welcome his holy will. In the apocryphal part of this book (<reference osisRef="Esth.4.17">ch. xiii. and xiv.</reference>) we have Mordecai's prayer and Esther's upon this occasion, and both of them very particular and pertinent. In the sequel of the story we shall find that God said not to this seed of Jacob, <hi type="italic">Seek you me in vain.</hi>  <chapter eID="Esth.4"/> <div eID="gen9028" type="x-p"/>

entries.41f991722d0e1d83115241b080650bcad210cb9e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4417"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 4</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Esth.4.1-Esth.4.14">Es 4:1-14</reference>. Mordecai and the Jews Mourn.</title> <div sID="gen6391" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4417"/><hi type="bold">1-2. When Mordecai perceived all that was done--</hi>Relying on the irrevocable nature of a Persian monarch's decree (<reference osisRef="Dan.6.15">Da 6:15</reference>), Hamman made it known as soon as the royal sanction had been obtained; and Mordecai was, doubtless, among the first to hear of it. On his own account, as well as on that of his countrymen, this astounding decree must have been indescribably distressing. The acts described in this passage are, according to the Oriental fashion, expressive of the most poignant sorrow; and his approach to the gate of the palace, under the impulse of irrepressible emotions, was to make an earnest though vain appeal to the royal mercy. Access, however, to the king's presence was, to a person in his disfigured state, impossible: "for none might enter into the king's gate clothed with sackcloth." But he found means of conveying intelligence of the horrid plot to Queen Esther. <div eID="gen6391" type="x-p"/>
entries.3199d7e0e779fb8eb5d716c923be43eb81bc5be3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4418"/><div sID="gen6392" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4418"/><hi type="bold">4. Then was the queen ... grieved; and ... sent raiment to ... Mordecai--</hi>Her object in doing so was either to qualify him for resuming his former office, or else, perhaps, of fitting him to come near enough to the palace to inform her of the cause of such sudden and extreme distress. <div eID="gen6392" type="x-p"/>
entries.b833b66032065c6fbaf3364485a930c902d5c2bd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4419"/><div sID="gen6393" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4419"/><hi type="bold">5. Then called Esther for Hatach, one of the king's chamberlains, whom he had appointed to attend upon her--</hi>Communication with the women in the harem is very difficult to be obtained, and only through the medium of the keepers. The chief eunuch receives the message from the lips of the queen, conveys it to some inferior office of the seraglio. When the commission is executed, the subaltern communicates it to the superintendent, by whom it is delivered to the queen. This chief eunuch, usually an old man who has recommended himself by a long course of faithful service, is always appointed by the king; but it is his interest, as well as his duty, to ingratiate himself with the queen also. Accordingly, we find Hatach rendering himself very serviceable in carrying on those private communications with Mordecai who was thereby enabled to enlist Esther's powerful influence. <div eID="gen6393" type="x-p"/>
entries.24421b14329546db10c8f1e8854174c69524a06e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4420"/><div sID="gen6394" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4420"/><hi type="bold">8. charge her that she should go in unto the king--</hi>This language is exceedingly strong. As it can scarcely be supposed that Mordecai was still using authority over Esther as his adopted daughter, he must be considered as imploring rather than commanding her, in the name of her brethren and in the name of her God, to make a direct appeal to the feelings of her royal husband. <div eID="gen6394" type="x-p"/>
entries.b6c3a97e8f775a4d040bb8cb1a8e459a0aa20da3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4421"/><div sID="gen6395" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4421"/><hi type="bold">11. whosoever, whether man or woman, shall come unto the king into the inner court, who is not called--</hi>The Persian kings surrounded themselves with an almost impassable circle of forms. The law alluded to was first enacted by Deioces, king of Media, and afterwards, when the empires were united, adopted by the Persians, that all business should be transacted and petitions transmitted to the king through his ministers. Although the restriction was not intended, of course, to apply to the queen, yet from the strict and inflexible character of the Persian laws and the extreme desire to exalt the majesty of the sovereign, even his favorite wife had not the privilege of entree, except by special favor and indulgence. Esther was suffering from the severity of this law; and as, from not being admitted for a whole month to the king's presence, she had reason to fear that the royal affections had become alienated from her, she had little hope of serving her country's cause in this awful emergency. <div eID="gen6395" type="x-p"/>
entries.10bab8f5ba6082647f0315a47a5bead7e8956efd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4422"/><div sID="gen6396" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4422"/><hi type="bold">13-14. Then Mordecai commanded to answer Esther--</hi>His answer was to this effect, that Esther need not indulge the vain hope she would, from her royal connection, escape the general doom of her race--that he (Mordecai) confidently believed God would interpose, and, if not through her, by some other deliverer, save His people; but that the duty evidently devolved on her, as there was great reason to believe that this was the design of Providence in her elevation to the dignity of queen, and therefore that she should go with a courageous heart, not doubting of success. <div eID="gen6396" type="x-p"/>
entries.70b021a8e84af19367ae344b789ba2535677dddb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4423"/><div sID="gen6397" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4423"/><hi type="bold">16. so will I go in unto the king, which is not according to the law--</hi>The appeal of Mordecai was irresistible. Having appointed a solemn fast of three days, she expressed her firm resolution to make an appeal to the king, though she should perish in the attempt.<div eID="gen6397" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6398" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I ... and my maidens--</hi>It is probable that she had surrounded herself with Jewish maidens, or women who were proselytes to that religion. <chapter eID="Esth.4"/>

entries.00753806133a665b6445d44c85e1c02a2709ef42: <div eID="gen15516" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen15517" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen15518" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen15518" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen15517" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen15519" type="x-p"/> On hearing the king's decree to exterminate the Jews, Mordecai mourns, and clothes himself in sackcloth, <reference osisRef="Est.4.1">Est 4:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Est.4.2">Est 4:2</reference>. The Jews are filled with consternation, <reference osisRef="Est.4.3">Est 4:3</reference>. Esther, perceiving Mordecai in distress at the palace gate, sends her servant Hatach to inquire the reason, <reference osisRef="Est.4.4-Est.4.6">Est 4:4-6</reference>. Hatach returns with the information, and also the express desire of Mordecai that she should go instantly to the king, and make supplication in behalf of her people, <reference osisRef="Est.4.7-Est.4.9">Est 4:7-9</reference>. Esther excuses herself on the ground that she had not been called by the king for thirty days past; and that the law was such that any one approaching his presence, without express invitation, should be put to death, unless the king should, in peculiar clemency, stretch out to such persons the golden scepter, <reference osisRef="Est.4.10-Est.4.12">Est 4:10-12</reference>. Mordecai returns an answer, insisting on her compliance, <reference osisRef="Est.4.13">Est 4:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Est.4.14">Est 4:14</reference>. She then orders Mordecai to gather all the Jews of Shushan, and fast for her success three days, night and day, and resolves to make the attempt, though at the risk of her life, <reference osisRef="Est.4.15-Est.4.17">Est 4:15-17</reference>. <div eID="gen15519" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15520" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen15520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15521" type="x-p"/> Mordecai rent his clothes - He gave every demonstration of the most poignant and oppressive grief. Nor did he hide this from the city; and the Greek says that he uttered these words aloud: Αιρεται εθνος μηδεν ηδικηκος, A people are going to be destroyed, who have done no evil!
entries.5623098f5d70ba422738f35459b3327e578b24f1: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen15521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15522" type="x-p"/> Before the king's gate - He could not enter into the gate, of the place where the officers waited, because he was in the habit of a mourner; for this would have been contrary to law.
entries.f219e19ef053a6a7e03d28dc9b6a623c170841ba: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen15522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15523" type="x-p"/> Fasting, and weeping, and wailing - How astonishing, that in all this there is not the slightest intimation given of praying to God!
entries.e16e79a4b0cf9d7424083962e81e0bc07f429ad6: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen15523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15524" type="x-p"/> Sent raiment - She supposed that he must have been spoiled of his raiment by some means; and therefore sent him clothing.
entries.97ad7072936794c5289d770689c1c9d15fa59001: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen15524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15525" type="x-p"/> Then called Esther for Hatach - This eunuch the king had appointed to wait upon her, partly, as is still the case in the East, to serve her, and partly, to observe her conduct; for no despot is ever exempt from a twofold torture, jealousy and suspicion.
entries.676d2493253966bcc7b4bb3e84a2b98549f63ece: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen15525" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15526" type="x-p"/> That she should go in unto the king - The Greek adds, "Remember the time of your low estate, and in what manner you have been nourished, and carried in my arms; and that Haman, who is next to the king, has got a decree for our destruction. Pray, therefore, to the Lord, and plead with the king, that we may be delivered from death." But there is not a word of this either in the Hebrew, Syriac, or Vulgate.
entries.a9895f42e46552da8f3288167c548c45fe4218f7: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen15526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15527" type="x-p"/> Into the inner court - We have already seen that the Persian sovereigns affected the highest degree of majesty, even to the assuming of Divine honors. No man nor woman dared to appear unveiled before them, without hazarding their lives; into the inner chamber of the harem no person ever entered but the king, and the woman he had chosen to call thither. None even of his courtiers or ministers dared to appear there; nor the most beloved of his concubines, except led thither by himself, or ordered to come to him. Here was Esther's difficulty; and that difficulty was now increased by the circumstance of her not having been sent for to the king's bed for thirty days. In the last verse of the preceding chapter we find that the king and Haman sat down to drink. It is very likely that this wicked man had endeavored to draw the king's attention from the queen, that his affection might be lessened, as he must have known something of the relationship between her and Mordecai; and consequently viewed her as a person who, in all probability, might stand much in the way of the accomplishment of his designs. I cannot but think that he had been the cause why Esther had not seen the king for thirty days.
entries.11632e923eb95968363a336de7d6a6ffc916c6a1: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen15527" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15528" type="x-p"/> Think not - that thou shalt escape - This confirms the suspicion that Haman knew something of the relationship between Mordecai and Esther; and therefore he gives her to understand that, although in the king's palace, she should no more escape than the Jews.
entries.578e4874b0d58749adfeef7112108b2b583f2e25: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen15528" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15529" type="x-p"/> Then shall there enlargement and deliverance arise - He had a confidence that deliverance would come by some means; and he thought that Esther would be the most likely; and that, if she did not use the influence which her providential station gave her, she would be highly culpable. <div eID="gen15529" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15530" type="x-p"/> And who knoweth whether thou art come - As if he had said, "Is it likely that Divine providence would have so distinguished thee, and raised thee from a state of abject obscurity, merely for thy own sake? Must it not have been on some public account! Did not he see what was coming? and has he not put thee in the place where thou mayest counteract one of the most ruinous purposes ever formed?" Is there a human being who has not some particular station by an especial providence, at some particular time, in which he can be of some essential service to his neighbor, in averting evil or procuring good, if he be but faithful to the grace and opportunity afforded by this station? Who dares give a negative to these questions? We lose much, both in reference to ourselves and others, by not adverting to our providental situation and circumstances. While on this subject, I will give the reader two important sayings, from two eminent men, both keen observers of human nature, and deeply attentive in all such cases to the operations of Divine providence: - "To every thing there is a season; and a time to every purpose under heaven. Therefore withhold not good from them to whom it is due, when it is in the power of thy hand to do it." <div eID="gen15530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15531" type="x-p"/> Solomon. <div eID="gen15531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15532" type="x-p"/> There is a tide in the affairs of men, <div eID="gen15532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15533" type="x-p"/> Which, taken at the flood, leads on to fortune; <div eID="gen15533" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15534" type="x-p"/> Omitted, all the voyage of their life <div eID="gen15534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15535" type="x-p"/> Is bound in shallows, and in miseries. <div eID="gen15535" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15536" type="x-p"/> Shakespeare. <div eID="gen15536" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15537" type="x-p"/> Has there not been a case, within time of memory, when evil was designed against a whole people, through the Hamans who had poisoned the ears of well-intentioned men; in which one poor man, in consequence of a situation into which he was brought by an astonishing providence, used the influence which his situation gave him; and, by the mercy of his God, turned the whole evil aside? By the association of ideas the following passage will present itself to the reader's memory, who may have any acquaintance with the circumstance: - "There was a little city, and few men within it; and there came a great king against it, and besieged it, and built great bulwarks against it. Now there was found in it a poor wise man, and he by his wisdom delivered the city; yet no man remembered that same poor man!" "Then said, I, Ah, Lord God! They say of me, Doth He Not Speak Parables?" Rem acu tetigi.
entries.fbd52ffa217084b886db6f3e90abcc2fd2718f43: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen15537" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15538" type="x-p"/> Fast ye for me, and neither eat nor drink three days - What a strange thing, that still we hear nothing of prayer, nor of God! What is the ground on which we can account for this total silence? I know it not. She could not suppose there was any charm in fasting, sackcloth garments, and lying on the ground. If these were not done to turn away the displeasure of God, which seemed now to have unchained their enemies against them, what were they done for? <div eID="gen15538" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15539" type="x-p"/> If I perish, I perish - If I lose my life in this attempt to save my people, I shall lose it cheerfully. I see it is my duty to make the attempt; and, come what will, I am resolved to do it. She must, however, have depended much on the efficacy of the humiliations she prescribed.  <chapter eID="Esth.4"/> <div eID="gen15539" type="x-p"/>

entries.306532d277bd51bdf729be9a0a3925cb3b7d0191: <reference osisRef="Esth.4.1">Est 4:1</reference> <div eID="gen6738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6739" type="x-p"/> Mordochai learnt all that was done, - not only what had been openly proclaimed, but, as is shown by <reference osisRef="Esth.4.7">Est 4:7</reference>, also the transaction between the king and Haman. Then he rent his garments, put on sackcloth and ashes, and went out into the midst of the city, making loud and bitter lamentation. Comp. on the last words, Gen 27:34. The combination of אפר with שׂק ילבּשׁ is an abbreviation for: put on a hairy garment and spread ashes upon his head, in sign of deep grief; comp. <reference osisRef="Dan.9.3">Dan 9:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.2.12">Job 2:12</reference>, and elsewhere.
entries.1e6d019b0865beb9b9aef07778646ced2e04d001: <reference osisRef="Esth.4.2">Est 4:2</reference> <div eID="gen6739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6740" type="x-p"/> And came even before the king’s gate, i.e., according to <reference osisRef="Esth.4.6">Est 4:6</reference>, the open space before the entrance to the royal palace; for none might enter wearing mourning. לבוא אין, there is no entering, i.e., none may enter; comp. Ewald, §321, <hi type="italic">c</hi>.
entries.9a622458173593953fe506a015335671c8e42d29: <reference osisRef="Esth.4.3">Est 4:3</reference> <div eID="gen6740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6741" type="x-p"/> Also in every province whither the king’s decree arrived, there arose a great mourning among the Jews. אשׁר מקום is an adverbial <hi type="italic">accusat</hi>. <hi type="italic">loci</hi> in apposition to בּכל־מדינה: in every place to which the word of the king and his decree reached, i.e., arrived. “Sackcloth and ashes were spread for many,” i.e., many sat in hairy garments upon the earth, where ashes had been spread; comp. Isa 58:5. The meaning is: All the Jews broke out into mourning, weeping, and lamentation, while many manifested their grief in the manner above described.
entries.43085b369fd00e3448a3db8c036a0aafc6b9c43b: <reference osisRef="Esth.4.4">Est 4:4</reference> <div eID="gen6741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6742" type="x-p"/> The matter was made known to Esther by her maids and eunuchs, i.e., by her attendants. The <hi type="italic">Chethiv</hi> תּבואינה does not elsewhere occur after ו consecutive, hence the substitution of the <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> תּבואנה. The object of יגּידוּ: what they told her, is evidently, from what follows, the circumstance of Mordochai’s appearance in deep mourning before the gate of the palace. On receiving this information the queen fell into convulsive grief (תּתחלחל, an intensive form of חוּל, to be seized with painful grief), and sent to Mordochai raiment to put on instead of his sackcloth, evidently for the purpose of enabling him to enter the palace and give her the particulars of what had happened. But Mordochai did not accept the raiment.
entries.300da9c70c33cd882660636588bc7c5c72105b16: <reference osisRef="Esth.4.5-Esth.4.7">Est 4:5-7</reference> <div eID="gen6742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6743" type="x-p"/> Then Esther sent Hatach, one of the eunuchs whom the king had set before her, i.e., appointed to attend her, to Mordochai to learn ”what this, and why this,” i.e., what was the meaning and the cause of his thus going about in mourning. When Hatach came forth to him in the open place of the city before the king’s gate, Mordochai told him all that had happened, and the amount of the money which Haman had promised to weigh to the king’s treasures (i.e., to pay into the royal treasury) for the Jews, to destroy them, i.e., that it might be permitted him to destroy the Jews. פּרשׁה, properly a determined, accurate statement, from פּרשׁ in the sense of to determine clearly (see rem. on <reference osisRef="Lev.24.12">Lev 24:12</reference>); here, according to the context: amount, sum. This promise of Haman is here emphatically mentioned as the chief point, not so much for the purpose of raising the indignation of Esther to the highest pitch (Bertheau), as to show the resentment and eagerness with which Haman had urged the extermination of the Jews. The <hi type="italic">Chethiv</hi> יהוּדיּים is the rarer form for יהוּדים, and is repeated <reference osisRef="Esth.8.1">Est 8:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Esth.8.7">Est 8:7</reference>,<reference osisRef="Esth.8.13">Est 8:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Esth.9.15">Est 9:15</reference>, Est 9:18.
entries.b146fd62a53fb06256e828afdb3e5326ed8376f8: <reference osisRef="Esth.4.8">Est 4:8</reference> <div eID="gen6743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6744" type="x-p"/> Mordochai also gave Hatach a copy of the decree published in Susa (בּשׁוּשׁן נתּן, like <reference osisRef="Esth.3.15">Est 3:15</reference>) to show it to the queen. The להּ וּלהגּיד following is more correctly drawn towards the subsequent וּלצוּות, as by Bertheau, than connected according to the accentuation with what precedes. Before this infinitive must be supplied from the context, especially from <reference osisRef="Esth.4.7">Est 4:7</reference> : and Mordochai commissioned him or told him (Hatach): to declare unto her and to command her (Esther) to go in unto the king, to entreat him and to make request before him for her people. על בּקּשׁ, to beg, to make request for something, like Ezr 8:23, and Est 7:7. עמּהּ על, concerning her people, i.e., in this connection: for them.
entries.9f593547ce6da1567ec10bcaed8ec7b5153faf20: <reference osisRef="Esth.4.9-Esth.4.11">Est 4:9-11</reference> <div eID="gen6744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6745" type="x-p"/> When Hatach brought this information to Esther, she sent word by him to Mordochai, that she might not go in unto the king unsummoned. אל מ תּצוּהוּ, she ordered or commissioned him to Mordochai, viz., to tell him what follows, <reference osisRef="Esth.4.11">Est 4:11</reference> : “All the king’s servants and the people of the king’s provinces (i.e., all the officers and subjects of the king) know, that with respect to every man or woman that shall come in unto the king, into the inner court, that is not called - one (the same) law (is) for him: to put (him) to death, except him to whom the king shall hold out the golden sceptre, that he may live.” לואשּׁה כּל־אישׁ precede as <hi type="italic">nominativi absol.;</hi> these are followed by two relative clauses, which are succeeded by the anacoluthic predicate דּתו אחת: one and the same law is for him (דּתו, the law concerning him, the unsummoned appearer, the matter of which is briefly stated by להמית). In the inner court dwelt the king, seated on his throne (comp. <reference osisRef="Esth.5.1">Est 5:1</reference>). The law, that every one entering unbidden should be put to death, was subject to but one exception: וגו מאשׁר לבד, except him to whom the king stretches out, etc. הושׁיט from ישׁט, appearing only in the present book (<reference osisRef="Esth.5.2">Est 5:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Esth.8.4">Est 8:4</reference>), but frequently in Chaldee and Syriac, signifies to hold out, to extend, with לו, to or towards him. שׁרביט, the Aramaic form for שׁבט, sceptre. Access to the royal presence had been already rendered difficult by an edict issued by Dejokes the Mede, Herod. 1:9; and among the Persians, none, with the exception of a few individuals (Herod. iii. 118), were permitted to approach the king without being previously announced (Herod. iii. 140; Corn. Nepos, <hi type="italic">Conon</hi>, 3). Any one entering unannounced was punished with death, unless the king, according to this passage, gave it to be understood by stretching forth his sceptre that he was to remain unpunished. It is, however, self-evident, and the fact is confirmed by Herod. iii. 140, that any who desired audience were allowed to announce themselves. Esther might, it seems, have done this. Why, then, did she not make the attempt? The answer lies in her further message to Mordochai: “and I have not been called to come in unto the king these thirty days.” From these words it appears, that formerly she had been more frequently summoned before the king. Now, however, a whole month had passed without any invitation. Hence she concluded that the king did not much wish to see her, and for this reason dared not go unto him unbidden. Evidently, too, she was unwilling to be announced, because in that case she would have been obliged immediately to make known to the king the cause of her desiring this interview. And this she would not venture to do, fearing that, considering the great favour in which Haman stood with the king, she might, if she did not provoke his displeasure against herself through her intercession for her people, at least meet with a rejection of her petition. To set aside an irrevocable decree sealed with the king’s seal, must have appeared to Esther an impossible undertaking. To have asked such a thing of the king would have been indeed a bold venture.
entries.fbfbaa9ca2e165080b7282fad42167146ee4e577: <reference osisRef="Esth.4.12-Esth.4.14">Est 4:12-14</reference> <div eID="gen6745" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6746" type="x-p"/> When what Esther said was reported to Mordochai, he sent word back to her (השׁיב): “Think not in thy soul (with thyself) to be saved in the house of the king above all the Jews; for if thou holdest thy peace at this time, recovery and deliverance will arise from another place, but thou and thy father’s house shall be destroyed. And who knows if thou hast attained to royalty for a time such as this?” By the words: “Think not that thou wilt be saved in the king’s house above all the Jew,” i.e., alone of all the Jews, Mordochai does not reproach Esther with being indifferent to the fate of her fellow-countrymen, but rather calls her attention to the fact that her own life is in danger. This is evident from the clause: if thou hold thy peace, will not intercede with the king for thy people, help will come from some other quarter. רוח = רוחה, <reference osisRef="Exod.8.11">Exo 8:11</reference>, ἀναψύξις, deliverance from oppressive restraint. יעמוד, rise up, arise, used according to later custom for קוּם, as in 1Ch 20:4. The thought is: the Jewish nation cannot perish, its continuance is guaranteed by the divine promise. If thou wilt venture nothing for its safety, God will bring deliverance, but destruction will come upon thee and thy family. Though Mordochai neither speaks of God, nor alludes directly to His assistance, he still grounds his hopes of the preservation of his people upon the word and promise of God, and Brentius pertinently remarks: <hi type="italic">habes hic excellentem ac plane heroicam Mardochaei fidem, qua in praesentissimo ac periculosissimo discrimine videt futuram liberationem.</hi> The last clause of <reference osisRef="Esth.4.14">Est 4:14</reference> is by most expositors understood as saying: and who knows whether thou hast not for a time like this attained to royalty? This agrees with the sense, but cannot be verbally justified, for אם does not mean whether not. The sentence contains an aposiopesis. The clause depending on the conditional אם is unspoken, but understood. Besides, הגּעתּ is not in the imperfect. Hence it can only be translated: Who knows, if thou hadst not attained to royalty at or for such a time? Then the clause omitted would be: what thou then wouldst have done. יודע מי more frequently has the meaning of <hi type="italic">perhaps</hi>; and Mordochai says: perhaps thou hast attained to royalty (to the dignity of queen) for a time like this, sc. to use thy position for the deliverance of thy people. In the turn thus given to the sentence it contains the most urgent injunction to Esther to use her high position for the preservation of her fellow-countrymen.
entries.2bff40878ba231bd9bf5f274a60930f9254a07e3: <reference osisRef="Esth.4.15-Esth.4.16">Est 4:15-16</reference> <div eID="gen6746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6747" type="x-p"/> This pressing monition produced its result. Esther returned answer to Mordochai: “Go, gather together all the Jews that are found in Susa, and fast ye for me: I also and my maidens will fast; and so will I go to the king against the law; and if I perish, I perish.” Esther resolves to go to the king unsummoned, but begs Mordochai and all the Jews to unite in a three days’ fast, during which she and her maidens will also fast, to seek by earnest humiliation God’s gracious assistance in the step she proposes to take, for the purpose of averting the threatened destruction of her people. “Though 'God' and 'prayer' are not here mentioned, it is yet obviously assumed that it was before God that the Jews were to humble themselves, to seek His help, and to induce Him to grant it. 1Ki 21:27-29; <reference osisRef="Joel.1.14">Joe 1:14</reference>; Jon 3:5.” (Berth.). To designate the strictness of this fasting, the words: “neither eat nor drink,” are added. The “three days, night and day,” are not to be reckoned as three times twenty-four hours, but to be understood of a fast which lasts till the third day after that on which it begins; for according to <reference osisRef="Esth.5.1">Est 5:1</reference>, Esther goes to the king on the third day. Comp. the similar definition of time, Jon 2:1. The addition “day and night” declares that the fast was not to be intermitted. וּבכן, and in thus, i.e., in this state of fasting. כּדּת לא אשׁר: which is not according to law. לא אשׁר is used, like the Aramaean form לא דּי, in the sense of <hi type="italic">without</hi> (comp. Ewald, §222, <hi type="italic">c</hi>): without according to law = contrary to law. The last words: “if I perish, I perish,” etc., are the expression not of despair, but of resignation, or perfect submission to the providence of God; comp. Gen 43:14.
entries.33d4942538d5b466cc27ea23fa7f0ac1dea5b6f1: <reference osisRef="Esth.4.17">Est 4:17</reference> <div eID="gen6747" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6748" type="x-p"/> And Mordochai went his way, i.e., from the place before the court of the king, to do what the queen had commanded him to do. Esther’s Gracious Reception by the King. Haman’s Rage against Mordochai - <reference osisRef="Esth.5.1-Esth.5.14">Est 5:1-14</reference> <div eID="gen6748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6749" type="x-p"/> On the third day Esther betook herself in her royal apparel to the inner court of the palace, and was so kindly received by the king, that he promised to grant her any petition she might make; whereupon she requested the king to come with Haman that day to a banquet which she had prepared (<reference osisRef="Esth.5.1-Esth.5.8">Est 5:1-8</reference>). On returning from this banquet, Haman saw Mordochai in the king’s gate, and when the latter did not bow before him, was so enraged, that, upon the advice of his wife and friends, he resolved to induce the king to permit the execution of Mordochai on the following day (<reference osisRef="Esth.5.9-Esth.5.14">Est 5:9-14</reference>).  <chapter eID="Esth.4"/> <div eID="gen6749" type="x-p"/>

entries.72a8848174b978d8fd73a3a1a96e217a01f30a7f:
<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="4" type="chapter">
                  <ns0:head>CHAP. IV.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1 WHen Mordecai perceived all that was done, Mordecai rent his clothes, and put on sackcloth with ashes, and went out into the midst of the city, and cried with a loud and bitter cry <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Partly to express his deep sense of the mischief coming upon his people: partly to move the pity of others to do what they could to prevent it: and partly that by this means it might come to the Queens ear.</ns0:note>:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 And came, even before the kings gate; for none <ns0:hi>might</ns0:hi> enter into the kings gate <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">And therefore he might not sit there, as he had hitherto done.</ns0:note> clothed with sack<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cloth <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Left is should give the King any occasion of grief or trouble.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 And in every province whithersoever the kings commandment, and his decree came, <ns0:hi>there was</ns0:hi> great mourning among the Jews, and fasting, and weeping, and wailing, and <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> sack<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cloth and a his were laid under many.</ns0:note> many lay in sackcloth and ashes.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 So Esthers maids, and her <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> chamberlains came and told <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> her. Then was the queen exceedingly grie<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ved, and she sent raiment to cloth Mordecai <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">That so he might be capable of returning to his former place, if not of coming to her to acquaint her with the cause of that unu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sual sorrow.</ns0:note>, and to take away his sackcloth from him: but he <ns0:hi>received it</ns0:hi> not.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 Then called Esther for Hatach, <ns0:hi>one</ns0:hi> of the kings chamberlains, <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. whom he had set be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore her.</ns0:note> whom he had appointed to attend upon
<ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:379" />
her; and gave him a commandment to Mordecai, to know what it <ns0:hi>was,</ns0:hi> and why it <ns0:hi>was.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 So Hatach went forth to Mordecai, unto the street of the city, which <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> before the kings gate.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 And Mordecai told him of all that had happened unto him, and of the sum of mony that Haman had promised to pay to the kings treasuries for the Jews, to destroy them.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 Also he gave him the copy of the writing of the decree, that was given at Shushan to destroy them, to shew <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> unto Esther, and declare <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> unto her, and to charge her <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Not only in his own name, to whom she manifested a singular respect, though his relation to her was yet unknown, but also in the name of the great God.</ns0:note> that she should go in unto the king, to make supplication unto him, and to make request be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore him for her people.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9 And Hatach came and told Esther the words of Mordecai.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10 Again Esther spake unto Hatach, and gave him commandment to say unto Mordecai;</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11 All the kings servants, and the people of the kings provinces do know <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">By common <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ame of this received custom and law.</ns0:note>, that whosoever, whether man or woman, shall come unto the king into the in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ner court <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">With<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />in which, the Kings residence and throne was in. This was decreed, partly to maintain both the Majesty, and the safety of the Kings person: and partly by the contrivance of the greater officers of state, that few or none might have access to the King but them<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />selves and their friends. And many such severe laws there were in the Persian Court, which profane Historians relate, as that if any person looked upon one of the Kings Concubines, or wore any of his own clothes, or drunk of that water which he had appropriated to himself, and other such like things, he was punished with death.</ns0:note>, who is not called, <ns0:hi>there is</ns0:hi> one law of his to put <ns0:hi>him</ns0:hi> to death <ns0:hi>m,</ns0:hi> except such to whom the king shall hold out the golden scepter that he may live: but I have not been called to come in unto the king, these thirty days <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Which gives me just cause to suspect and fear that the kings af<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fections are alienated from me, and therefore that neither my per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />son nor petition will be acceptable to him.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12 And they told to Mordecai Esthers words.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13 Then Mordecai commanded to answer Esther, Think not with thy self that thou shalt escape in the kings house <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Being, or because thou art in the Kings house, and an eminent member of his family.</ns0:note>, more than all the Jews:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="14">14 For if thou altogether holdest thy peace at this time, <ns0:hi>then</ns0:hi> shall there <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>respi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ration.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> enlargement and deliverance arise to the Jews from another place <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">From another land, and by another means; which God can, and I am fully persuaded, will raise up.</ns0:note>
                     <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> but thou and thy fathers house shall be destroyed <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">By the righteous and dreadful judgment of God, punishing thy cowardize, and self-see<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />king, and thy want of love to God, and to his and thy own peo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple.</ns0:note>: and who know<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth whether thou art come to the kingdom for <ns0:hi>such</ns0:hi> a time as this <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">It is probable God hath raised thee to this honour for this very season: and therefore go on couragiously, and doubt not of the success.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">15 Then Esther bad <ns0:hi>them</ns0:hi> return Mordecai <ns0:hi>this an<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />swer,</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="16">16 Go, gather together all the Jews <ns0:hi>that are</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>found.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sent in Shushan, and fast ye <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">And pray; which was the main business, to which fasting was only an help and an handmaid.</ns0:note> for me, and neither eat nor drink <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">To wit, so as you use to do, ei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther deliciously or plentifully. Leave off your common meals, din<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ners by day, and suppers at night, and eat and drink no more than meer necessity requires; that so you may give your selves to con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stant and servent prayers, for which your ordinary repasts will un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fit you. For it is not likely that she would impose the burden of absolute fasting so long upon all the Jews, which very few of them were able to endure. And so the like phrase is taken, <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 27. 33. where he saith, <ns0:hi>This is the fourteenth day that ye have continued fasting, having taken nothing.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> three days, night or day: I also and my maidens <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Which she had chosen to attend upon her person, and were doubtless either of the Jewish nation, or prosely<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ted by her, or others means to that Religion.</ns0:note> will fast likewise <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Which may be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />long, either 1. To the thing only, that as they did fast, so she would. Or rather, 2. To the time of three days and three nights; for so she might do, though she went to the King <ns0:hi>o<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap> the third day.</ns0:hi> For the fast began at evening, and so she might continue her fast three whole nights, and two whole days and the greatest part of the third; a part of a day being reputed a <ns0:hi>day</ns0:hi> in the account of Scripture and other Authors: of which see on <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 12. 40. Yea, she might fast all that day too: for it is probable she went not to the King till he had dined; when she supposed she might find him in the most mild and pleasant humour, and then returned to her apartment, where she fasted till the evening.</ns0:note>, and so will I go in unto the king, which <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> not according to the law <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Which is a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gainst the law now mentioned.</ns0:note>, and if I perish, I perish <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Although my danger be great and evident considering the expressness of that law, and the uncer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tainty of the Kings mind, and that severity which he shewed to my predecessor <ns0:hi>Vashti;</ns0:hi> yet rather than neglect my duty to God and to his people, I will go to the King, and cast my self chearfully, and resolutely upon Gods providence for my safety and success.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="17">17 So Mordecai <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>
                           <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                              <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> went his way, and did according to all that Esther had commanded him.</ns0:p>
               </ns0:div>
